5x-vs-3x-cleaning-price.html.text:
← Janitorial bid calculator

5× vs 3× commercial cleaning: why 60% of today’s price is not the 3-day bid

Contractors search this because a facility manager who wants fewer visits usually offers a linear cut: 3 days instead of 5, so pay 60%. That sounds fair if every dollar of the bid were labor. It is not.

Labor hours do drop with the visits. A 2.4-hour clean five days a week is about 52 hours a month; three days a week is about 31. The loaded wage on those hours scales the same way.

Travel, equipment, and the monthly supply line stay. The van still goes to the building. The auto-scrubber is still assigned to the account. Paper, liners, and chemicals in a per-square-foot monthly model do not disappear because Tuesday and Thursday came off the calendar. Overhead is a markup on that whole direct cost, not only on labor.

On a typical 8,000 sq ft office — restrooms, break room, lobby, $17 wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin — a 5-day bid is about $1,720 a month. Sixty percent of that is $1,032. The 3-day price that still holds 20% is about $1,069. The gap looks small until travel climbs: at $800 a month for equipment and drive time, the same linear 60% offer loses money outright.

5× / week3× / week, priced rightLinear 60%
Labor hours / month52.031.231.2
Price that holds 20%$1,720$1,069$1,032
Same bid with $800 travel$2,834$2,184$1,700 (under water)

Open the janitorial bid calculator, enter your own wage, burden, and travel, and set current days / proposed days. It shows the 3-day price that still holds your margin, the margin left if you take their linear number, and a reply you can paste. Nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not advice. It does not tell you to accept or refuse a renewal. Confirm scope, insurance, and payroll before you send a number.

Common questions

If a client cuts cleaning from 5 days to 3, should the monthly price drop 40%?

No. Labor hours scale with visits, but travel, equipment, and a monthly supply line stay on the job. The price that still holds your target margin is higher than 60% of the 5-day price.

How do I price a 3-day commercial cleaning schedule from a 5-day bid?

Recalculate labor hours at the new weekly frequency, keep equipment, travel, and monthly supplies, then reapply overhead and margin. A production-rate bid calculator does that without guessing a square-foot discount.

FOR COMMERCIAL CLEANING CONTRACTORS

Bid the building, not the square footage.

Price a janitorial contract the way the trade actually does: each space divided by the production rate your crew really hits, optional day-porter shifts priced as scheduled coverage, then wage burden, supplies, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the monthly price, what it works out to per square foot and per labor hour, the number below which the job loses money, what a 5×-to-3× schedule cut is actually worth — not 60% of today’s price — whether letting the building buy the paper still holds your margin, and whether throwing in the takeover clean still leaves a first month.

Taking a second building? See whether it still pays after the drive.

The building

One row per space type. Add an optional proposal name when you need scope detail such as "Second-floor restrooms". Production rate is cleanable square feet one cleaner covers per hour — pick a space type to start from a common figure, then replace it with a rate timed from your own crew. A space that is not on the list (gym, server room, loading dock) is Other space: name it so the labor split and the copied bid say what you actually clean.

Day porter / scheduled shifts

Optional. A day porter is a person on site during business hours, not extra square feet on the night clean. Hours = people × hours per shift × shifts per week × 52/12. Leave the wage blank to use the cleaner rate below; fill it in when the porter is paid more.

RolePeopleHours / shiftShifts / weekHourly wage

One-time / project work

Strip and wax, carpet extraction, and the initial deep clean are invoiced once. Pricing them inside the monthly contract is how a contractor works eleven months at a loss after the building is caught up. Hours = square feet ÷ production rate × coats or passes.

Project typeSq ftSq ft / hourCoats / passesMaterials $

Periodic services

Quarterly floor care, twice-a-year extraction, annual windows — a lump cost per visit, spread across the year. This is not strip-and-wax project work (priced once from square feet). Cost × occurrences ÷ 12 goes into the monthly contract, including after a 5× to 3× schedule cut.

ServiceCost / occurrenceTimes / year

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off — the part of a cleaner’s cost that never shows up on their pay rate. Underestimating it is the most common reason a janitorial bid that looked profitable was not.

If they cut the schedule

A prospect who asks for 3 days a week instead of 5 will often offer 60% of the current monthly price. Labor hours do drop with the visits. Supplies, equipment, and travel stay on the job, so the price that still holds your margin is higher than a linear cut. Why 60% of a 5-day price is not a 3-day bid.

If they want to buy the paper

A facility manager who says “we’ll buy the paper, soap, and liners — take the supplies off” is not asking you to drop the whole line. Restroom stock is only a share of it. Chemicals, finish, and glass stay yours. And if they run out, the emergency fill you still make can cost more than stocking it yourself. Should I let the building buy the paper?

If they want the initial thrown in

A neglected or vacant building’s first visit is several regular cleans of labor plus extra chemicals. Prospects ask to “just include it.” Month 1 then carries a project on a periodic price — and if they cancel after 30 days, that giveaway is the whole relationship. Should I throw in the initial clean?

      Common bidding questions

      How do I price a day porter on a janitorial contract? Price the person, not the floor. Hours = people × hours per shift × shifts per week × 52/12, then the same loaded wage, overhead, and margin as the night clean. An 8-hour weekday porter is about 173 hours a month — usually more labor than the entire after-hours production clean.

      Should I bake the day porter into the monthly cleaning price? No. The night clean is production-rate work; the day porter is coverage during business hours. Combining them hides how much of the bid is a body on site. This calculator keeps the two numbers separate and adds them into one monthly contract price.

      How do I price strip and wax with a janitorial contract? Treat it as one-time project work. Hours are the floor area divided by a production rate, times the number of finish coats. Add finish, stripper, and pads as materials. Keep that total off the monthly service price so you are not giving away eleven months of wax after the first invoice.

      Should the initial deep clean be in the monthly price? Usually no. An initial or post-construction clean is a different production rate and a one-time invoice. Mixing it into the recurring bid is how a contract that looked fine in month one loses money for the rest of the year.

      Why not bid the whole building by square foot? Restrooms, kitchens, and exam rooms take several times the labor of open office. Two 8,000 sq ft buildings can differ by 30% in hours. The labor split is there so that mix is visible before the price goes out.

      Common questions

      How do I price a day porter on a janitorial contract?

      Price the day porter as scheduled coverage: people × hours per shift × shifts per week × 52/12, then the same loaded wage, overhead, and margin as the night clean. Do not convert the porter into extra square feet or a faster production rate.

      Should I bake the day porter into the monthly cleaning price?

      No. The night clean is production-rate work; the day porter is a person on site during business hours. Combining them hides how much of the bid is coverage.

      How do I price strip and wax with a janitorial contract?

      Treat strip and wax as one-time project work invoiced separately from the monthly service so the remaining months are not underpriced.

Does the second building still pay after the drive?

should-i-let-them-buy-the-paper.html.text:
← Janitorial bid calculator

Should I let the building buy the paper, soap, and liners?

Contractors search this because a facility manager who wants to buy restroom stock usually offers a simple trade: they take paper, soap, and liners, you drop the supplies line. That sounds fair if every dollar of that line were restroom stock. It is not.

Restroom stock is only a share of the supplies line. On a typical office bid, paper, soap, liners, and seat covers are about 65% of the monthly per-square-foot supplies number. Chemicals, floor finish, and glass cleaner stay yours. Labor, the van, and the auto-scrubber do not move.

Dropping the whole line is the they-buy-everything price. Overhead and margin sit on that line too. Taking “the supplies off” today’s bid is the labor-only number, not the restroom-handoff number.

If they run out, you still fill. An emergency restock plus leftover cases is less efficient than stocking the closet yourself. On the default 8,000 sq ft office — $17 wage, 28% burden, $0.005 / sq ft supplies, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, $35 emergency fill — you-supply is $1,720.00. They-buy-restroom-stock is $1,682.62. Dropping the whole line is $1,662.50. If you still emergency-fill, the price that holds 20% is $1,732.94 — $12.94 a month above you-supplying.

Open the janitorial bid calculator, keep your own wage, burden, and supplies rate, and set the restroom-stock share plus the emergency fill. It shows the handoff price that still holds your margin, the margin left if you drop the whole line, and a reply you can paste. Nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not advice. It does not tell you to accept or refuse a handoff. Confirm what they will actually stock, who buys when they run out, and your own supply invoices before you send a number.

Common questions

If the building buys the paper, soap, and liners, should I drop the supplies line?

No. Restroom stock is only a share of a monthly supplies line. Chemicals, floor finish, and glass stay yours. Dropping the whole line from today's price is the they-buy-everything number, not the restroom-handoff number.

Can letting them buy the paper cost more than supplying it myself?

Yes, if you still emergency-fill when they run out. A restock trip plus leftover cases is less efficient than stocking the closet yourself, so the monthly price that holds your margin can land above the you-supply bid.

should-i-throw-in-the-initial-clean.html.text:
← Janitorial bid calculator

Should I throw in the initial clean to win the monthly?

Contractors search this because a facility manager who wants the building brought back from vacant or neglected usually offers a simple trade: do the deep clean, keep the monthly you already quoted. That sounds cheap if the first visit were just another Tuesday. It is not.

A takeover clean is a project, not a regular visit. Dust on vents, baseboards, behind furniture, extra restroom detail, and leftover construction grit take several regular cleans of labor plus extra chemicals. On a typical 8,000 sq ft office — $17 wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin — one regular visit is 2.4 hours. A 5× takeover is 12.0 hours plus $80 of extra supplies.

Throwing it in at today’s monthly loses money in month 1. The periodic price ($1,720.00) was built on $1,376.00 of monthly cost. The takeover adds $392.29 of cost. Month 1 walk-away is $1,768.29. Keep today’s monthly and month 1 loses $48.29.

If they cancel after 30 days, that giveaway is the job. Invoice the initial and a one-month stay still leaves $442.07. Throw it in and the same 30 days finish $48.29 under water. Baking it into the monthly over 12 months is $1,760.86 — $40.86 above today — and does not help if they leave after month 1.

Bake it into the monthly over 12 months$0.00$1,760.86still month-1 loss if they leave

Open the janitorial bid calculator, keep your own wage, burden, and production rates, and set how many regular visits the initial is worth. It shows the one-time that still holds your margin, the monthly if you bake it in, the month-1 loss if you throw it in, and a reply you can paste. Nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not advice. It does not tell you to invoice, amortize, or refuse the giveaway. Confirm the building’s actual condition, who stays after 30 days, and your own payroll before you send a number.

Common questions

Should I throw in the initial clean to win a janitorial contract?

Not at today's monthly unless you can stand to lose money in month 1. A neglected 8,000 sq ft office's 5× takeover (12 labor hours plus $80 of extra supplies) is a $490.36 one-time if it still holds a 20% margin. Throwing it into a $1,720 monthly loses $48.29 in month 1 against a $1,768.29 walk-away.

What if they cancel after 30 days?

The giveaway is then the whole relationship. On the same default office the thrown-in first month finishes $48.29 under water, versus $442.07 if the initial was invoiced as a one-time. Baking it into the monthly over 12 months is $1,760.86 — $40.86 above today's monthly — and still does not help if they leave after month 1.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Janitorial Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

"20 cents a square foot" is not a price for a building — it is a price for one specific mix of open office, restrooms, and common area, quietly applied to the next building whether or not its mix looks anything like the first one's.

What a flat per-foot rate is

A flat rate is the fastest way to quote: multiply total cleanable square footage by a number and read off a monthly price. Prospects like it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it needs no walkthrough to quote over the phone. It is also the number a prospect holding a competitor's proposal will ask you to match.

The rate was set on one building — one particular split of open office, private offices, restrooms, and common area — and then reused for the next building's square footage, whether or not that building's mix looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each space type's cleanable square footage, its own production rate, and cleanings per week, plus your loaded wage and payroll burden, supplies, equipment, overhead, and target margin. It turns each space's own labor hours into a price, and reports the price per square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this building's actual mix, not a generic one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether a 10,000 sq ft building is 5% restrooms or 20% restrooms — a several-times difference in restroom labor for the same total floor area. Prices each space type at its own production rate, so a restroom-heavy building's extra labor shows up in the price instead of being averaged away into one blended rate.
Assumes the building the rate was set on is the building being quoted, with no way to tell when the mix has changed. On two otherwise identical 10,000 sq ft buildings cleaned 5×/week, prices the 5%-restroom building at about $2,386/month and the 20%-restroom building at about $2,948/month — a 24% difference the square footage alone never showed.
Carries a rate set on a light-restroom building over to a heavier one at the same square footage: $0.2386/sq ft × 10,000 sq ft = $2,386/month. Reports the heavier building's own walk-away cost ($2,506/month) and target-margin price ($2,948/month) — the carried-over flat quote lands about $120/month under walk-away and $562/month short of the target margin.
Bakes payroll burden into a round rate nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the contract is signed.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when the building's mix has moved away from the one the rate was set on, and nothing about a per-square-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get janitorial bids wrong?

Because labor hours come from a space's production rate, not from its square footage alone. A restroom takes several times the labor per square foot of open office, so a building's mix of space types -- not just its total floor area -- decides how many hours the contract actually needs. A flat rate charges every building the same for a given square footage and is wrong on most of them.

Can two buildings the same size really cost differently to clean?

Yes. Take two 10,000 sq ft buildings cleaned 5 nights a week with the same wage, burden, supplies, overhead, and target margin -- one that is 5% restrooms and one that is 20% restrooms. This calculator prices the 5%-restroom building at about $2,386 a month and the 20%-restroom building at about $2,948 a month: a 24% difference on identical square footage, from the restroom share alone.

What happens if a rate set on one building is quoted on another?

On the pair above, the $0.2386-per-square-foot rate that holds the target margin on the light-restroom building comes to $2,386 a month if quoted on the heavy-restroom building's identical 10,000 square feet -- about $120 a month under that building's own walk-away cost of $2,506, and about $562 short of the price that would actually hold the target margin there. The flat rate does not know which building it was set on.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar buildings -- close to the same restroom, office, and common-area mix -- a flat rate can land close. The risk is carrying a rate set on one building's mix over to a building with a different one, because the square-footage total looks the same either way and nothing about the rate itself says the mix has changed.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the square footage, production rate, and cleanings per week you enter for each space, plus your wage, burden, supplies, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price, a walk-away cost, and a price per square foot for the building you describe -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until a building's mix stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $2,386, $2,948, $2,506, and $562 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on the two example buildings described in this page, not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs.

Open the Janitorial Bid Calculator and price your own contract.

vs-cleanguru.html.text:
← Janitorial Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. CleanGuru

Two different shapes: CleanGuru is account-based bidding, work-loading, invoicing, and mobile-checklist software for a cleaning company's whole client roster. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one contract cost, before you sign up for anything.

What each tool is for

CleanGuru is bidding and business-management software built for commercial cleaning and janitorial contractors. Its bid calculator generates a price recommendation from work-loading formulas and a cost-plus model factoring wages, payroll taxes, overhead, and target margin; a mobile app lets a rep enter room measurements during a walkthrough and price on the spot; and the platform adds invoicing, mobile checklists, and separate modules for residential maid, carpet, window, tile, and move-in/out cleaning. It is account-based — you sign in to use it. CleanGuru's own site was not reachable for live verification in the session that wrote this page, and no dollar figure or plan name for it is stated anywhere here: only its well-documented identity and category, from its own public product pages, are described.

This calculator does none of what CleanGuru does. It stores no client roster, sends no invoice, and keeps no mobile checklist. It takes one contract's spaces — cleanable square footage, production rate, and cleanings per week for each — plus loaded wage, payroll burden, supplies, equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per square foot per month, the annual contract value, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It also prices day-porter shifts and one-time project work (strip and wax, extraction, an initial deep clean) separately from the monthly service, and answers three renewal questions with their own table and pasteable reply: a schedule cut from 5× to 3× a week, the client buying their own paper and restroom supplies, and throwing in the initial clean. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need one account running bids, proposals, invoicing, and mobile checklists across my whole client roster.CleanGuru, or comparable janitorial bidding software — that is not something this calculator does.
What should I charge for this one contract, from its space types and production rates, before I sign up for anything?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
A client wants to cut from 5× to 3× a week and offers 60% of today's price — is that fair?This calculator's 5× vs 3× comparison, built on this contract's own labor split, not a generic rate.
They'll buy their own paper and restroom supplies if I drop that line — what's a fair price cut?This calculator's buy-the-paper comparison.
They want the initial deep clean thrown in with month one — what does that cost me?This calculator's initial-clean comparison.
I want mobile bidding I can walk a building with on my phone, plus invoicing and checklists for every account I run.CleanGuru or comparable software — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that.
Do I need to create an account or sign in to use the tool?This calculator: no. CleanGuru: yes, it is account-based software.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or CleanGuru?

They do different jobs, and a cleaning contractor of any size will likely end up touching both. CleanGuru is bidding, work-loading, invoicing, and mobile-checklist software sold to commercial cleaning and janitorial contractors, with a bidding calculator, a mobile app for walking a building and entering measurements on the spot, and modules for janitorial, residential maid, carpet, window, tile, and move-in/out cleaning. It is account-based — you sign in to use it. This calculator does one narrower thing, free and with no account: starting from each space's cleanable square footage and production rate, cleanings per week, loaded wage and payroll burden, supplies, equipment, overhead, and target margin, it prices one janitorial contract, reports the walk-away price below which the job loses money, and answers three renewal questions contractors get asked — a schedule cut from 5× to 3× a week, the client buying their own paper and supplies, and throwing in the initial deep clean — each with a table and a pasteable reply. A contractor who wants one account running bids, proposals, invoicing, and mobile checklists across a whole client roster is better served by CleanGuru or comparable janitorial bidding software; a contractor who wants an instant, private price and margin check on one contract, before opening any account, is in the right place here.
